In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine..why: The first base-pairing rule taught in biology; stated verbatim hundreds of times and in Wikipedia.

sources.quote: The nitrogenous bases of the two separate polynucleotide strands are bound together, according to base pairing rules (A with T and C with G), with hydrogen bonds to make double-stranded DNA.

In DNA, thymine pairs with adenine..why: The same base-pairing rule read from thymine's side; the Thymine article states it, and the pair is named in both orders throughout biology text.

sources.quote: In DNA, thymine (T) binds to adenine (A) via two hydrogen bonds, thereby stabilizing the nucleic acid structures.

sources.note: The same pair stated from adenine's side.

In DNA, the base that pairs with the bas.why: People say that ATP contains adenine and, separately, that adenine pairs with thymine, but nobody calls adenine 'the base of ATP' when giving the pairing rule, so the two lessons are never joined in one sentence; the answer is worked out from two common statements.

sources.query: pairs with the base in ATP

sources.note: Approximate co-occurrence (AND, max_clause_freq 500000); not statements of the fact, which needs the adenine step.

ATP contains the base adenine..why: Part of the definition of ATP (adenosine triphosphate).

sources.quote: From the perspective of biochemistry, ATP is classified as a nucleoside triphosphate, which indicates that it consists of three components: a nitrogenous base (adenine), the sugar ribose, and the triphosphate.

The deoxyribonucleoside of the base that.why: People say adenine pairs with thymine and, in another context, that thymine's nucleoside is thymidine, but nobody describes thymidine as the nucleoside of 'the base that pairs with adenine'; the pairing and the nucleoside name are common separate premises, their combination is not something anyone writes.

sources.note: Nucleoside-level pairing statements, not the description asked.

The deoxyribonucleoside of thymine is th.why: Standard nucleoside naming, stated in the Thymine and Thymidine articles.

sources.quote: Thymine combined with deoxyribose creates the nucleoside deoxythymidine, which is synonymous with the term thymidine.

DNA is a double helix..why: Stated verbatim nearly two thousand times.

sources.quote: Deoxyribonucleic acid (; DNA) is a polymer composed of two polynucleotide chains that coil around each other to form a double helix.

DNA is a protein..why: Deliberately false side fact for the disjunction: DNA is a nucleic acid, not a protein.

sources.quote: Deoxyribonucleic acid (; DNA) is a polymer composed of two polynucleotide chains that coil around each other to form a double helix.

Thymine is a pyrimidine..why: Thymine is classed as a pyrimidine base in every account of the nucleobases (purines A and G, pyrimidines C, T and U); the Thymine article's first sentence says so. Exact-phrase counts are low but the sentence is the standard textbook classification.

sources.quote: Thymine is also known as 5-methyluracil, a pyrimidine nucleobase.

The base that pairs with adenine in DNA.why: The class of thymine is stored by name; the base is reached here only through adenine's DNA partner, so it rests on the removed pair.

sources.quote: Thymine is also known as 5-methyluracil, a pyrimidine nucleobase.

notes: Dev ABox contraction paired with biology-replace-d001: removes that revision's original fact, 'In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine' (same subject, relation pairs_with and old object). pairs_with is tagged symmetric and cardinality:many (staging/biology.RELATIONS.md; reading: among natural bases a base has one partner within one kind of duplex, but synthetic analogues can add partners, so it is not functional; the same tag the paired expansion biology-insert-d001 needs, since with 'functional' its extra partner for guanine would be a hidden revision). Tag note: the revision's related near uses the one-natural-partner reading for guanine in DNA (cytosine gives way when adenine takes guanine); the revision's own notes call the relation 'functional', which the catalogue does not, so that wording is the revision's, not this record's. The cardinality question is the many-valued case: 'In RNA, does adenine pair with uracil?' (yes before and after). It is a cross-context case: adenine's partners differ by duplex type (thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA), so removing the DNA pair says nothing about the RNA pair; within DNA alone the relation acts as one-partner, which is why the question asks the other duplex. Evidence for the RNA pair: 132 Dolma hits for 'adenine pairs with uracil' and the Uracil article ('In RNA, uracil base-pairs with adenine and replaces thymine during DNA transcription'), copied from the revision record (same fact, same evidence); the validator takes no evidence key for a contraction cardinality question, so it is recorded here only. Own questions (direct, paraphrase, cross-lingual from the revision, propositional under strong Kleene) become 'does not know'. Related near reads the removed pair from thymine's side (symmetry; stored, Thymine article). Related far was rewritten after review: the earlier question ('in RNA, is adenine's DNA partner replaced by uracil?') could be answered 'yes' from the kept facts 'adenine pairs with uracil in RNA' and 'uracil replaces thymine', so it was no longer determinate. It now asks a property only thymine has, reached through adenine's DNA partner and without RNA or uracil: the group at position 5 of its ring (a methyl group), 2 hops through the stored bridge 'thymine has a methyl group at position 5' (checked before editing). Stored evidence: 287 Dolma hits for 'methyl group of thymine', 780 for '5-methyluracil' and the Thymine article's first sentence. Derived: the cardinality question above, and the two 2-hop questions through the removed fact, the revision's binding through ATP's base (ATP contains adenine) and its deoxyribonucleoside composition (thymidine becomes 'does not know'). Known confound, recorded: pairing over the four DNA bases is a closed system, so the kept pair 'guanine pairs with cytosine' lets a model rebuild A-T by elimination, and the kept RNA facts (adenine-uracil, uracil replaces thymine) are another route back to thymine; a model that rebuilds the pair has not contracted it (AGM success), so a 'thymine' or 'methyl group' answer is weak evidence of failed removal, as for the other two derived questions. Unrelated near asks guanine's partner, the untouched pair of the same relation (cytosine); contraction is exempt from Rule 7. Evidence for the shared facts is copied from the revision record. Re-check on 2026-11-12: every infini-gram count in the six biology contraction and expansion records was asked again (47 distinct queries across the six records, 0 mismatched); Wikipedia quotes are copied from the revision records or from the articles' first sentences, and the Wikipedia search API answered HTTP 429 when this revision was written, so no new search could be run. Revision 2026-11-12 (model audit): all four models missed the earlier related far ('Which chemical group is attached at position 5 of the ring of the base that pairs with adenine in DNA?', answers: phosphate group, nitrogenous base, uracil, thymine), a wording problem since the fact itself (thymine is 5-methyluracil) is held. It now asks the plain yes/no question 'Does the base that pairs with adenine in DNA carry a methyl group?' (yes before, not known after), through the bridge 'Thymine carries a methyl group' (check: 'Does thymine carry a methyl group?'); evidence for both is the thymine methyl-group evidence kept above (287 and 780 exact-phrase hits, Thymine article), and the infini-gram count for the new sentence 'thymine carries a methyl group' is 0, so the claim rests on the other phrases. The earlier description of the position-5 question above is superseded. Revision 2026-11-13 (model audit, second round): three models still missed the methyl-group question ('No', 'No', 'Thymine'), so it was replaced rather than reworded. Related far now asks 'Is the base that pairs with adenine in DNA a pyrimidine?' (yes before, not known after) through the bridge 'Thymine is a pyrimidine' (check: 'Is thymine a pyrimidine?'); evidence: Dolma 33 for 'thymine is a pyrimidine', 28 for 'thymine, a pyrimidine', and the Thymine article's first sentence ('a pyrimidine nucleobase'). The methyl-group question and its evidence are superseded.
